shell.tagline: One question per page, answered from figures that Eurostat, the OECD and the ECB publish themselves. Nothing is estimated on top, and every number is traceable to its source.
shell.disclaimer: Not medical advice. Informational comparison only.

methodBlock.intro: Every number on this page is either published by Eurostat or counted from those published numbers. Nothing is estimated on top.
methodBlock.whatItIsBody: Eurostat publishes one indicator per country per year: the age by which half of young people no longer live in a household with their parents. It is derived from the European Union Labour Force Survey. Eurostat’s own dataset title calls it an “estimated average age”, which does not match its own definition — a midpoint and an average are different things, and they differ most where the distribution is lopsided. This page follows the definition.
methodBlock.whatItIsNotBody: It is not a distribution, so no percentile can be calculated from it. It is not a count of people. And it is a country-level figure: it describes a cohort, not any individual in it.
methodBlock.coverageStale: {names} stopped reporting earlier and are shown at their most recent year, hatched on the map and labeled in the table.
methodBlock.coverageNotInDataset: The United States, Canada and Australia are not in this dataset, because Eurostat does not cover them.
methodBlock.breakBody: In {break} Eurostat flags a break in the series: the European Labour Force Survey was reorganized, and {withBreak} of {all} countries carry the flag for that year. The break year itself is transitional, so figures before {since} exist in the source but are not comparable with today. Comparisons over time on this page start in {since}.

method.shortVersionWeDo: Short version: we do not make any up. Every figure is published by a statistical agency, and the only arithmetic we add is the kind you could repeat.
method.aFigureIsNot: A figure is not the same as a distribution
method.mostStatisticalAgenciesPublish: Most statistical agencies publish one number per country per year. That number tells you where the middle of a country sits. It does not tell you how people are spread around that middle, and no amount of arithmetic can recover the spread from the summary once it has been thrown away.
method.menAndWomenNever: men and women, never a total
method.theCountryOutlinesOn: The country outlines on the maps. Public domain, pinned to one package version and one checksum, projected once by a script in the repository rather than by hand.
method.whatEachSourcePublishes: What each source publishes, in its own words
method.oneBlockPerDataset: One block per dataset: the code you can look it up by, how far the figures reach, what we read per country, and when it was last refreshed. Nothing here is typed by hand — it is read from the files the pipeline writes.
method.thePagesThemselvesCalculate: The pages themselves calculate every sentence from that committed JSON at build time. There is no number typed into a page by hand anywhere on this site, which is the only way a figure cannot quietly go stale when a source republishes.
method.theGateDoesNot: The gate does not trust the file we built. It goes back to the source response and recomputes.
method.whatWeWillNot: What we will not do, and what we cannot

about.aSmallProjectWith: A small project with one rule
about.hiIMSimeon: Hi, I’m Simeon. I built HumanAverage on my own, around one rule: no number appears on this site unless it can be traced back to data somebody else published.
about.searchForAEuropean: Search for a European average and you get a number. It is usually correct, and it is almost useless on its own — because one figure for a continent hides the thing you actually wanted to know: how far apart the countries are, and where you sit between them.
about.whoMakesItAnd: Who makes it, and who does not
about.thereIsNoAnonymous: There is no anonymous “research team” either, and no medical team, research institute or editorial department. It is one person. Where software or AI helps prepare the work, I remain responsible for the final check, the choice of sources and the decision to publish.
about.iNeverInventA: I never invent a statistic. Every figure comes from a dataset I can point to.
about.iSayWhichKind: I say which kind of figure a page shows, and never call something a percentile when the source published a single number instead of a distribution.
about.iShowNoPercentile: I show no percentile where no representative sample exists, however tempting.
about.iKeepMyOwn: I keep my own calculation separate from results published by others.
about.iDescribeWhatA: I describe what a comparison means, and what it does not.
about.iCorrectDemonstrableErrors: I correct demonstrable errors and say when the method was last checked.
about.humanaverageIsFreeTo: HumanAverage is free to use. Advertising may eventually help cover hosting and further development. It currently carries no advertising code, and adverts would never change a calculation or a conclusion.
about.thisSiteIsAn: This site is an informational comparison. It is not medical advice, not a diagnosis, and not an assessment of your health.
about.answeringTakes: Answering that takes the figure for every country rather than the one for the whole, the honesty to say which side of it you fall on rather than inventing a precision the source does not support, and a check that the numbers survived the trip from the agency to the page. That is what this site does, and the
about.notPartOfAny: I am not part of any government, statistical agency, university or institution, nobody commissions or reviews what goes on it, and I have no relationship with the agencies whose figures I use — Eurostat, the OECD and the European Central Bank — beyond downloading what they publish for anyone.
about.ifYouCanShow: If you can show that something here is wrong, that is genuinely useful and it will be fixed. Email
about.forAQuestion: . For a question about a specific result, mentioning which page you were on, the country you picked and the figure you entered helps.

privacy.whatYouTypeIs: What you type is never sent to us. The comparison is calculated inside your own browser, from a data file your browser already downloaded with the page.
privacy.thePagesAskFor: The pages ask for a country and one number — the age you left home, the hours you work, what your household is worth. Those values stay in the memory of the page you have open. They are used to look up a position in a table that was downloaded with the page, and they disappear when you reload or close it. Nothing is transmitted to us, and no account is created.
privacy.onTheEuropeanComparison: On the European comparison pages there is one exception. The country and the age you enter, together with the light or dark theme you pick, are saved in this browser's local storage, under a single key, so that the next page already knows them instead of asking again. That storage sits on your own device: it is never sent to us, there is no server behind it, and no profile of you exists anywhere else. Clearing site data for this domain removes it, and a private window keeps nothing at all.
privacy.thisSiteSetsNo: This site sets no cookies, runs no analytics, and contains no advertising code. There is nothing to consent to, so we do not ask.
privacy.thatMayChangeIf: That may change. If analytics or advertising is ever added, this page will be updated before the code goes live, and where consent is legally required it will be requested through an appropriate consent platform — with no non-essential cookies set before you have chosen.
privacy.weDoAlsoUse: We do also use Google Search Console, which reports how the site performs in Google Search. It shows aggregated figures — how often pages appeared and were clicked — and does not identify individual visitors to us.
privacy.weLinkToThe: We link to the CDC, to scientific publishers and to source datasets. Once you open one of those, that party's own privacy policy applies. We never pass your entered values along in such a link.
privacy.whereAPageOffers: Where a page offers to copy your result, what lands on your clipboard is a short piece of text: your own figure, the published figure it was compared against, and the address of the page. No link carries your values in the web address, and nothing is sent anywhere — the copy happens in your browser and stops there. What you then paste, and to whom, is yours to decide.
privacy.asWithVirtually: As with virtually any website, the hosting provider processes technical request data: an IP address, the time, the page requested, browser information and errors. This is necessary to deliver the site securely. HumanAverage is hosted by
privacy.weReceiveYour: we receive your address, your message and anything else you choose to include, and use it only to handle your question. Email is processed through Gmail, so Google's privacy policy also applies. Please do not send passwords, medical records or other sensitive information.
privacy.becauseWeNever: Because we never receive your measurements, we cannot show you, correct or delete them — there is nothing on our side to act on. For questions about other data, about deleting an email you sent us, or about this policy, write to

contact.aSiteBuiltOn: A site built on a promise of traceable numbers only works if the numbers can be challenged. Corrections are welcome and get fixed.
contact.thereIsNoContact: There is no contact form, because a form would mean collecting your details on a site whose whole point is that it collects almost nothing.
contact.humanaverageCannotAnswerMedical: HumanAverage cannot answer medical, psychological or personal health questions, and nothing here is a diagnosis. If a measurement worries you, that is a conversation for a doctor, who can see everything a country-level statistic cannot.
contact.specificResultBody: the page, the country you chose, the value you entered and the answer you got back. That is enough to reproduce it exactly.
contact.aboutAWrongFigure: About a figure you think is wrong:
contact.wrongFigureBody: which number, and what you believe it should be. A source makes it far quicker to check — and if you are right, it gets corrected.
contact.brokenBody: your device, browser and what you did just before it broke.
contact.datasetBody: a link to the data itself, not to an article about it. What works best is a series an agency publishes per country and keeps updating.

notes.theMetricPagesAnswer: The metric pages answer one question each. These are the pieces that do not fit on them: where a dataset breaks, where a definition does not match its own title, and what that changes about the answer.
notes.aPieceAppearsHere: A piece appears here when a dataset does something that its own page cannot fully carry. The metric pages have room for a method section, not for an argument. When the argument is the interesting part, it moves here.
notes.whatDoesNotAppear: What does not appear here: anything the data cannot carry. No round-ups of other people's reporting, no predictions, and no sentence with a number in it that was typed by hand. Every figure in every piece is computed from the same files the metric pages use, at build time, so a piece cannot quietly go stale when a source publishes again.
notes.ofTheDatasets: Of the {datasets} datasets behind this site, {broken} carry a series break that the code refuses to measure across. That is the kind of thing worth a piece: it is invisible on the chart, it reverses a conclusion, and almost nobody checks for it.

home.title: A European average describes almost nobody.
home.lead: In {low} half of young people have left home by {lowAge}. In {high} that point does not arrive until {highAge} — {gap} years apart, on the same question. One European figure hides both.
home.everyFigureBelowSwitches: Every figure below switches to your country. Nothing you pick leaves your browser.
home.eachOneIsA: Each one is a map, a sortable table of every country, and a comparison with whatever you enter about yourself. The bar under each figure shows where it sits between the lowest and the highest country.
home.whatWeWorkedOut: What we worked out along the way
home.whereADatasetTurned: Where a dataset turned out to say something other than its title, we write it down rather than quietly work around it.
home.anAverageIsA: An average is a bad answer to a personal question
home.pageTitle: HumanAverage — European Figures, and Where You Fall
